title: What Netflix Would Look Like if an Edtech Company Built It
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer uses a Netflix comparison to criticize how edtech displays student data. Netflix works invisibly and actively by recommending what to watch next, whereas a typical edtech product offers loads of data and leaves the teacher to work out what to do, which he finds both overwhelming and passive. He cites Heather Hill's reading of the research that studying student data rarely improves outcomes, because data pinpoints gaps without telling teachers how to respond. His proposal, developed with colleagues at Amplify, is to drop the pie charts and scatter plots and give one confident recommendation for the 15-minute review after a digital assessment, such as asking students to write a question for which the most common wrong answer is correct. The underlying test he sets for edtech is whether it takes weight off teachers' shoulders or adds to it.
points: Most edtech data displays are overwhelming yet passive, supplying graphs without guidance on what to do next.
Studies reviewed by Heather Hill suggest examining student data rarely improves outcomes because it does not tell teachers how to respond.

Meyer proposes replacing dashboards with a single confident recommendation for the 15-minute post-assessment review, such as having students write a question that makes the common wrong answer correct.
Designers should serve the wide range of teacher capacity and ask whether each feature lightens or adds to teachers' load.
quotes: The typical approach in edtech to data display is a rare combination of overwhelming and passive. It offers you loads of data and doesn’t help you figure out what to do with it.
By contrast, Netflix’s approach is invisible and active, meaning Netflix doesn’t show you any data but it makes some active recommendations that I, personally, find pretty accurate.

Why doesn’t data analysis work? All three researchers explained that while data is helpful in pinpointing students’ weaknesses, mistakes and gaps, it doesn’t tell teachers what to do about them. Most commonly, teachers review or re-teach the topic the way they did the first time or they give a student a worksheet for more practice drills.

What if we threw away the pie charts, 3D scatter plots, and all the other over-determined representations of student learning and, like Netflix, made our most confident recommendation for those 15 minutes? “Here’s a movie you might like” could then become “Here’s a question you might ask.” Or, perhaps more specifically, “Here is the most common wrong answer from your last assessment. Ask your students to write a question where it is the right answer.

One of the best outcomes of Desmos Classroom merging with Amplify has been the pressure to think about supporting a huge group of teachers with very different capacities instead of a smaller group of very high-capacity early adopters. That change, more than any other, accounts for my recent heel-turn away from depictions of teaching as martyrdom, and over-determined frameworks for teaching.
The way Netflix uses data takes weight off my shoulders. The majority of edtech data displays only adds to it.
